sections.h: Solomon's rise and the building of the temple (1 Kings 1–8)
sections.b: Solomon comes to the throne through a palace struggle. When his older brother Adonijah claims the crown, Nathan the prophet and Bathsheba remind the dying David of an oath, and Solomon is anointed at Gihon (1 Kings 1). He secures the kingdom by removing Adonijah, Joab and Shimei and banishing Abiathar (1 Kings 2). At Gibeon he asks God for "a heart that listens" to judge the people, and his judgment between two mothers shows God's wisdom in him (1 Kings 3). His court, his twelve districts, his wealth and his learning are described as the fulfillment of the promises to Abraham (1 Kings 4). With cedar from Hiram of Tyre and a drafted labor force he builds the temple in seven years and his own palace in thirteen (1 Kings 5–7), and at the Feast of Booths he dedicates the house with a great prayer (1 Kings 8). The portrait is glorious, but small warnings run through it: an Egyptian wife, the high places, horses, forced labor, and promises with conditions.

common: Solomon asked God for wisdom rather than riches, and God gave him both.
Solomon wrote Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs.
uncommon: Some historians think Solomon came to power by a palace coup led by Nathan, Bathsheba and Zadok, and that the story of David's oath was written to justify it.
A Jewish tradition holds that Solomon was only twelve years old when he became king.

sections.h: Adonijah's bid and his death (1 Kings 1–2)
sections.b: Adonijah was David's fourth son, born at Hebron to Haggith (2 Samuel 3:4), and after Absalom's death probably the oldest living son. Handsome and never corrected by his father, he gathered chariots and runners like Absalom and held a feast at En-rogel with Joab, Abiathar and the king's sons (1 Kings 1:5–10). When Solomon was anointed, he fled to the altar and was spared on condition of good behavior (1 Kings 1:49–53). After David's death he asked Bathsheba to obtain Abishag, David's young attendant, as his wife. Solomon took this as a claim to the throne and had Benaiah kill him (1 Kings 2:13–25). Readers have long debated whether Adonijah was a rebel plotting a second time or an older brother who lost the throne and then his life to a ruthless rival. Adonijah himself admitted that the kingship came to Solomon "from the LORD" (1 Kings 2:15).

common: Adonijah's request for Abishag was a disguised claim to the throne.
uncommon: Adonijah may have been the rightful heir by custom, and the narrator may be quietly sympathetic to him.

sections.b: In David's last days the two chief priests took opposite sides: Abiathar backed Adonijah, and Zadok anointed Solomon at Gihon with the horn of oil from the tent (1 Kings 1:7–8, 1:39). Solomon spared Abiathar because he had carried the ark and shared David's hardships, but banished him to his fields at Anathoth, and Kings notes that this fulfilled the word spoken against Eli's house at Shiloh (1 Kings 2:26–27; 1 Samuel 2:27–36). Zadok became the sole chief priest (1 Kings 2:35), and his grandson Azariah heads Solomon's list of officials (1 Kings 4:2). From then on the high priesthood in Jerusalem stayed in Zadok's family until the 2nd century BC. Ezekiel limits priestly service at the altar to "the sons of Zadok" (Ezekiel 44:15), and the Dead Sea Scrolls community gave its priests the same title. Anathoth later produced the prophet Jeremiah, possibly a descendant of Abiathar (Jeremiah 1:1).
sections.refs: 1 Kings 1:7–8; 1 Kings 1:39; 1 Kings 2:26–27; 1 Kings 2:35; 1 Kings 4:2; 1 Samuel 2:27–36; Ezekiel 44:15; Jeremiah 1:1

uncommon: H. H. Rowley and others proposed that Zadok was the Jebusite priest of Jerusalem before David took the city.

sections.h: David's old age and death (1 Kings 1–2)
sections.b: Kings opens with David old and cold, unable to get warm, cared for by the young Abishag, and unaware that his son Adonijah has claimed the throne (1 Kings 1:1–11). Roused by Nathan and Bathsheba, he acts once more as king: he swears that Solomon will reign and orders his anointing at once (1 Kings 1:28–40), then bows on his bed in thanks (1 Kings 1:47–48). His last words to Solomon join the language of Moses and Joshua, "be strong ... keep the law," with hard instructions about Joab and Shimei and kindness for Barzillai's sons (1 Kings 2:1–9). He dies after forty years as king and is buried in the City of David (1 Kings 2:10–11). The rest of Kings remembers him as the model king whose heart was whole with the LORD (1 Kings 11:4; 1 Kings 15:3–5), the standard by which his sons are judged.

common: David's deathbed charge about Joab and Shimei shows a king settling old scores.
uncommon: Some readers think David's charge was meant to remove blood guilt and a curse from his house, not to take revenge.

sections.h: Bathsheba, mother of the king (1 Kings 1–2)
sections.b: Bathsheba's second appearance in the story is as a political actor. Coached by Nathan, she goes to the old king and reminds him of his oath that her son Solomon would reign (1 Kings 1:11–21), and after David swears it again she blesses him (1 Kings 1:31). Under Solomon she becomes the queen mother: when she comes to speak for Adonijah, the king rises, bows to her and sets a throne for her at his right hand (1 Kings 2:19). Whether she passed on Adonijah's request for Abishag innocently or knew how her son would hear it, the text does not say. Kings later names the mother of almost every king of Judah, and the queen mother, the gevirah, held real power (1 Kings 15:13). Jewish tradition connects her with the advice of a king's mother in Proverbs 31:1–9.

uncommon: Some readers think Bathsheba knew that Adonijah's request would cost him his life and passed it on for that reason.

sections.b: Nathan, who had told David "You are the man" (2 Samuel 12:7) and named the infant Solomon "Jedidiah" (2 Samuel 12:25), returns as a kingmaker. He warns Bathsheba that Adonijah's feast puts her life and Solomon's at risk, tells her what to say to David, and comes in after her to "make her words complete" (1 Kings 1:11–27). David then has Zadok and Nathan anoint Solomon at Gihon (1 Kings 1:32–45). Readers differ: some see a faithful prophet making sure God's choice is carried out, others a court politician steering a failing king. His sons appear among Solomon's officials (1 Kings 4:5).

sections.h: Joab's death at the altar (1 Kings 2)
sections.b: David's charge to Solomon names Joab first: he murdered Abner and Amasa in peacetime and "put that war blood on the belt at his waist" (1 Kings 2:5–6). When Adonijah is executed, Joab flees to the LORD's tent and holds the horns of the altar, refusing to come out. Solomon orders Benaiah to kill him there, saying that this removes from David's house the blood Joab shed without cause (1 Kings 2:28–34). The law did allow a deliberate murderer to be taken from the altar (Exodus 21:14). Readers ask whether Joab died for his old murders or for backing Adonijah; the narrator's remark that he had followed Adonijah "though he had not turned to follow Absalom" (1 Kings 2:28) leaves room for both.

uncommon: The Greek text says Joab had not followed Solomon, rather than Absalom, which makes his motive purely political.

sections.b: After making a treaty with Hiram of Tyre for cedar and craftsmen (1 Kings 5), Solomon begins the house in his fourth year, 480 years after the exodus (1 Kings 6:1). The building was modest in size, about 90 by 30 feet (27 by 9 meters) on the common cubit, with a porch, a great hall and a cube-shaped inner room, the most holy place, where two great olive-wood cherubim spread their wings (1 Kings 6). Its walls were carved with cherubim, palms and flowers and covered with gold. A second Hiram cast the bronze pillars Jakin and Boaz, the great Sea on twelve oxen, and ten wheeled stands (1 Kings 7). At the Feast of Booths the ark was brought in, the cloud of the LORD's glory filled the house, and Solomon prayed that God, whom the heavens cannot contain, would hear every prayer made toward it (1 Kings 8). The LORD's word in the middle of the building report makes his presence depend on obedience, not on the building (1 Kings 6:11–13).

common: Solomon's temple stood on the site of today's Temple Mount (the Dome of the Rock area) in Jerusalem.
uncommon: Some scholars think the temple was first a royal chapel attached to the palace, and only later became the one central sanctuary of all Israel.

claude.title: Claude's theory: the temple's design retells the exodus
claude.body: My own suggestion: the order of the building account follows Israel's journey. The stones are prepared far away and brought in silence (6:7), as the people were brought out of Egypt. The house's size doubles the tabernacle's (6:2), the wilderness shrine now settled. The ark comes last, carried in by the priests with only the tablets of Horeb inside (8:9), and the same cloud that filled the tabernacle fills the house (8:10–11; Exodus 40:34–35). The 480 years of 6:1 tie the building to the exodus at its very start. Scholars have long noticed the links between the tabernacle and temple accounts; reading the temple's construction as a deliberate replay of the exodus journey is my own proposal.

sections.b: 1 Kings shows Solomon's wisdom in three forms. It begins as a gift: at Gibeon he asks for "a heart that listens" to judge God's people and tell good from bad, and God grants a wise and understanding heart (1 Kings 3:9–12). It is shown first as justice, in the case of the two mothers, where the king finds the truth with no witnesses (1 Kings 3:16–28). It appears as good government in his officials and districts (1 Kings 4:1–28), and as learning: three thousand proverbs, a thousand and five songs, and knowledge of trees, animals, birds and fish, greater than the wisdom of the east and of Egypt (1 Kings 4:29–34). The same word, chokhmah, describes the bronze worker Hiram's skill (1 Kings 7:14), as it did Bezalel's (Exodus 31:3). Later chapters will test whether wisdom is enough to keep a king faithful (1 Kings 11).

common: Solomon was the wisest person who ever lived.
uncommon: Some scholars think 4:33 describes lists of plants and animals like Egyptian word lists, rather than proverbs about nature.

sections.b: Solomon's reign shows the monarchy growing into a state. His list of officials adds new offices to David's: a head of the district officers, a palace manager, the "king's friend" and a chief of forced labor (1 Kings 4:1–6). Twelve district officers supply the court in turn (1 Kings 4:7–19, 4:27–28). The king has horses and chariots in great numbers (1 Kings 4:26), drafts Israelites for labor in Lebanon (1 Kings 5:13–14), and judges from a throne in his own hall (1 Kings 7:7). Much of this is what Samuel warned a king would do (1 Samuel 8:11–17) and what Deuteronomy's law of the king forbids in excess: many horses, many wives, and great wealth (Deuteronomy 17:16–17). The reign that begins with wisdom carries the seeds of the complaint that will divide the kingdom (1 Kings 12:4).
sections.refs: 1 Kings 4:1–28; 1 Kings 5:13–16; 1 Kings 7:7; 1 Samuel 8:11–17; Deuteronomy 17:14–20; 1 Kings 12:4

sections.b: 1 Kings 4 gives the fullest picture of Solomon's state: chief officials, twelve districts that include the old Canaanite cities of the Jezreel valley (Taanach, Megiddo, Beth-shean), daily provisions for a large court, thousands of horses, and rule over all the kingdoms from the Euphrates to the border of Egypt (1 Kings 4:21, 4:24). Traditional scholars take the lists as archival and the summary of dominion as describing vassal states in a time when the great powers were weak. Minimalist and low-chronology scholars take the summaries as later idealization, noting phrases like "Beyond the River" (4:24) that sound like Persian administration. Middle-view scholars accept a real but smaller kingdom. The lists themselves, with officers known only as "son of Hur" or "son of Deker" and two of Solomon's sons-in-law among them, look like a genuine document rather than invention.

sections.h: Hiram the king and Hiram the bronze worker (1 Kings 5; 7)
sections.b: Two men named Hiram serve Solomon. Hiram king of Tyre, who had loved David, makes a treaty with Solomon, sends cedar and cypress from Lebanon by sea in rafts, and receives wheat and oil every year (1 Kings 5:1–12). Josephus quotes Tyrian historians who say Hiram son of Abibaal reigned thirty-four years and traded riddles with Solomon (Against Apion 1.106–127). The second Hiram, son of a widow of Naphtali and a Tyrian bronze worker, is filled with skill, understanding and know-how like Bezalel, and casts the pillars Jakin and Boaz, the Sea, the stands and all the bronze vessels (1 Kings 7:13–47). Chronicles calls him Huram-abi and says his mother was from Dan (2 Chronicles 2:13–14).

Solomon's prayer at the temple's dedication is one of the longest prayers in the historical books. He stands before the altar with hands raised to the heavens, then kneels (1 Kings 8:22, 8:54). He praises God as beyond compare and faithful to his promises, confesses that the highest heavens cannot contain him, and asks that God's eyes be open day and night toward the house where his name is (1 Kings 8:23–30). Then he lists seven situations, an oath, defeat, drought, plague, a foreigner's prayer, war and exile, and in each asks God to hear from heaven and forgive (1 Kings 8:31–53). The prayer made Jerusalem the direction of prayer: Daniel prays toward it from Babylon (Daniel 6:10), and Jews still face it. Its confession, "We have sinned. We have gone wrong. We have done evil" (1 Kings 8:47), entered Jewish penitential prayer.

common: Jews pray facing Jerusalem because of Solomon's prayer.

sections.h: The cloud fills Solomon's temple (1 Kings 8)
sections.b: When the priests set the ark in the inner room and come out, "the cloud filled the LORD's house," and the priests cannot stand to serve, because "the LORD's glory filled the LORD's house" (1 Kings 8:10–11). The scene repeats the dedication of the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34–35). Solomon's poem explains: the LORD who said he would live in the thick dark cloud of Sinai now has a princely house (1 Kings 8:12–13). Yet the prayer that follows insists that God dwells in the heavens (1 Kings 8:27, 8:30). Chronicles adds fire from heaven (2 Chronicles 7:1–3). Ezekiel will see this glory leave before the temple falls (Ezekiel 10:18–19).

Abiathar is spared because he carried the ark before David (1 Kings 2:26), and Solomon worships before it on his return from Gibeon (1 Kings 3:15). Its last journey is a short one: from David's tent in the City of David up to the temple, where the priests set it in the inner room beneath the wings of the cherubim, its poles still in place and visible from the holy place (1 Kings 8:1–8). Kings insists that nothing was in it but the two stone tablets Moses placed there at Horeb (1 Kings 8:9). After this the ark is hardly mentioned again in Kings, and its fate is never told.
sections.refs: 1 Kings 2:26; 1 Kings 3:15; 1 Kings 8:1–9; 1 Kings 8:21; 2 Chronicles 35:3; Jeremiah 3:16

sections.h: The great cherubim of the temple (1 Kings 6–8)
sections.b: In the inner room Solomon set two cherubim of olive wood covered with gold, each ten cubits (about 15 feet, 4.5 meters) tall, with wings of five cubits. Side by side they stretched from wall to wall, their inner wings touching above the ark (1 Kings 6:23–28; 8:6–7). Together they formed the throne of the invisible LORD, "who sits on the cherubim as his throne" (1 Samuel 4:4). Cherubim were also carved with palm trees and flowers on every wall and door (1 Kings 6:29–35) and on the bronze stands (1 Kings 7:29, 7:36), making the house a garden guarded as Eden was (Genesis 3:24).
sections.refs: 1 Kings 6:23–35; 1 Kings 7:29; 1 Kings 7:36; 1 Kings 8:6–7; 1 Samuel 4:4; Genesis 3:24

sections.h: The promise with a condition (1 Kings 2; 6; 8)
sections.b: In 1 Kings the promise of 2 Samuel 7 is repeated with an "if." David tells Solomon that God will keep his word "if your sons guard their way" (1 Kings 2:4); God tells Solomon that he will make good his word "if you live by my rules" (1 Kings 6:12); and Solomon prays that God will keep the promise "if only your sons guard their way" (1 Kings 8:25). At the same time Solomon claims the promise as fulfilled: God has made him a house (1 Kings 2:24), he sits on David's throne and has built the house for God's name (1 Kings 8:20). Scholars discuss whether the conditional form is a later layer, or whether the dynasty was promised forever while each king's share depended on his loyalty (Psalm 132:11–12).
sections.refs: 1 Kings 2:4; 1 Kings 2:24; 1 Kings 2:45; 1 Kings 6:12–13; 1 Kings 8:20; 1 Kings 8:25–26; 2 Samuel 7:12–16; Psalm 89:30–37; Psalm 132:11–12

sections.h: The end of Eli's line in Jerusalem (1 Kings 2)
sections.b: Abiathar, the great-great-grandson of Eli and David's priest since the massacre at Nob, backed Adonijah. Solomon spared his life but expelled him "out of the LORD's priesthood," and Kings says this fulfilled the word spoken at Shiloh against Eli's family (1 Kings 2:26–27; 1 Samuel 2:31–36). Zadok took his place (1 Kings 2:35). The story shows priests as political figures at court, anointing kings and choosing sides (1 Kings 1:7–8, 1:39), and it fixes the high priestly line in Jerusalem for centuries.
sections.refs: 1 Kings 1:7–8; 1 Kings 1:39; 1 Kings 2:26–27; 1 Kings 2:35; 1 Samuel 2:31–36; 1 Samuel 22:20

sections.h: Gihon, En-rogel and the temple mount (1 Kings 1–8)
sections.b: The opening chapters of Kings are set in a small city on the ridge above the Kidron valley. Adonijah's feast is at En-rogel, where the Kidron meets the Hinnom valley; Solomon is anointed at the Gihon spring, half a mile up the valley, and the noise carries between them (1 Kings 1:9, 1:33–41). Shimei must not cross the Kidron (1 Kings 2:37). Solomon then builds north of the old City of David, on the higher ground of the temple mount, with his palace between (1 Kings 6–7), and the ark is carried up from "the City of David, that is, Zion" (1 Kings 8:1). From then on Jerusalem is "the city you chose" (1 Kings 8:44, 8:48).
sections.refs: 1 Kings 1:9; 1 Kings 1:33–41; 1 Kings 2:37; 1 Kings 3:1; 1 Kings 8:1; 1 Kings 8:44; 1 Kings 8:48

sections.b: David orders Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet to anoint Solomon at Gihon, then to blow the ram's horn and cry "Long live King Solomon!" (1 Kings 1:34). Zadok takes the horn of oil from the sacred tent and does it, and the people follow Solomon back up into the city with music (1 Kings 1:39–40). Unlike Saul and David, anointed first in private by a prophet, Solomon is anointed in public by a priest, at his father's command, to settle a dispute. The rabbis drew from this that a king's son is anointed only when his succession is challenged (Bavli Horayot 11b).

sections.h: The temple dedicated at the Feast (1 Kings 8)
sections.b: Solomon assembles Israel "in the month of Ethanim, at the feast," the seventh month, the Feast of Booths (1 Kings 8:2). The festival, with the dedication, lasts "seven days and then seven days more," and the people go home on the eighth day blessing the king (1 Kings 8:65–66). Chronicles explains the two weeks as a week of dedicating the altar followed by the feast itself and a closing assembly (2 Chronicles 7:8–10). Synagogues read 1 Kings 8 on Sukkot. Jeroboam's rival feast in the eighth month (1 Kings 12:32–33) is meant to replace this one.

Foreigners help build the temple: Hiram of Tyre and his Sidonians cut the cedar, the men of Gebal shape the stones, and a half-Tyrian craftsman casts the bronze (1 Kings 5:6, 5:18; 7:13–14). In his dedication prayer Solomon asks God to hear the nokhri, the foreigner from a distant land who has heard of God's great name and comes to pray toward the house, "so all the earth's peoples will know your name and fear you" (1 Kings 8:41–43). Isaiah's "house of prayer for all peoples" (Isaiah 56:7) and Jesus' use of it (Mark 11:17) take up the same hope.
sections.refs: 1 Kings 5:6; 1 Kings 5:18; 1 Kings 7:13–14; 1 Kings 8:41–43; Isaiah 56:6–7; Mark 11:17

sections.b: The last and longest case in Solomon's prayer is exile: the people sin, as everyone does, are handed to an enemy and carried to a land far or near. If there they "take it to heart," confess, and pray toward their land, the city and the house, Solomon asks God to hear, forgive and make their captors pity them (1 Kings 8:46–53). Traditional readers see a king who knew the covenant's warnings (Deuteronomy 28:36, 28:64; Leviticus 26:33). Most critical scholars see the hand of writers in the Babylonian exile, for whom the temple was gone and prayer toward it was all they had. Either way, the prayer gave the exiles their words (Daniel 6:10; Daniel 9:4–19).
sections.refs: 1 Kings 8:46–53; Leviticus 26:33; Leviticus 26:40–45; Deuteronomy 28:36; Deuteronomy 30:1–5; Daniel 6:10; Daniel 9:4–19

sections.b: The Septuagint of 1 Kings, called 3 Kingdoms, differs more from the Hebrew than almost any other historical book. In 1 Kings 1:1–2:11 the main Greek manuscript, Codex Vaticanus, carries the kaige revision toward the Hebrew, so the Lucianic manuscripts are the better witness to the Old Greek. After 2:35 and 2:46 the Greek adds two collections of short notes about Solomon, the "miscellanies," which mostly repeat material from chapters 3–9. It lacks 6:11–14, moves the palace account (7:1–12) after the temple furnishings, places Solomon's short poem (8:12–13) after the prayer in a fuller form citing "the Book of the Song," and has different numbers in several places (6:1; 4:32). Scholars debate whether these differences reflect an older Hebrew text (Trebolle, Schenker) or Jewish interpretation in Greek (Gooding, van Keulen).
sections.refs: 1 Kings 2:35; 1 Kings 2:46; 1 Kings 6:11–14; 1 Kings 7:1–12; 1 Kings 8:12–13; 1 Kings 8:53; 1 Kings 6:1

sections.b: At Gibeon "the LORD showed himself to Solomon" in a dream in the night and invited him to ask for anything (1 Kings 3:5). Solomon's request for a listening heart and God's generous answer take up the whole dream; then "Solomon woke up. It had been a dream!" (1 Kings 3:15), words that echo Pharaoh's waking in Genesis 41:7. The dream fits a pattern known from Egypt and Mesopotamia, where kings report a god's promise received in sleep at a shrine. God appears to Solomon a second time in 1 Kings 9:2.

Solomon's first recorded act after securing the throne is to become Pharaoh's son-in-law (1 Kings 3:1). The marriage was an alliance with a weakened Egypt, probably of the 21st dynasty, and brought Gezer as a dowry (1 Kings 9:16). Solomon built Pharaoh's daughter her own house (1 Kings 7:8; 9:24). Kings mentions her five times and lists her first among the foreign wives who turned his heart (1 Kings 11:1). Deuteronomy's warning against a king who sends the people back to Egypt for horses and takes many wives (Deuteronomy 17:16–17) hangs over the alliance.
sections.refs: 1 Kings 3:1; 1 Kings 7:8; 1 Kings 9:16; 1 Kings 9:24; 1 Kings 11:1; Deuteronomy 17:16–17

sections.b: 1 Kings 6:1 dates the start of the temple to the 480th year after the exodus and the 4th year of Solomon, usually reckoned as 967/966 BC. Read literally, this puts the exodus about 1446 BC, the "early date." Scholars who favor a 13th-century exodus read 480 as twelve generations of forty years, a schematic figure; the Greek has 440 years and Josephus 592. See the note on 1 Kings 6:1.

sections.h: The temple as the chosen place (1 Kings 3; 8)
sections.b: Before the temple, "the people kept offering sacrifices at the high places" because no house had yet been built for the LORD's name (1 Kings 3:2), as Deuteronomy allowed until the LORD gave rest and chose a place (Deuteronomy 12:9–11). Solomon presents the temple as that place: God has given rest (1 Kings 5:4; 8:56), and the house is where his name will be (1 Kings 8:16, 8:29). Chronicles, and probably a Qumran fragment, make the choice of Jerusalem explicit (2 Chronicles 6:5–6). From now on Kings judges kings by whether they remove the high places.
sections.refs: 1 Kings 3:2–4; 1 Kings 5:4–5; 1 Kings 8:16; 1 Kings 8:29; 1 Kings 8:44; 1 Kings 8:56; Deuteronomy 12:9–11; 2 Chronicles 6:5–6

sections.b: Solomon begins his reign with three executions, all carried out by Benaiah: Adonijah for asking for Abishag, Joab for the murders of Abner and Amasa and for backing Adonijah, and Shimei for leaving Jerusalem in breach of his sworn agreement (1 Kings 2:25, 2:34, 2:46). The text appeals to the law of blood guilt (1 Kings 2:31–33; Numbers 35:33) and the limits of altar asylum (Exodus 21:14). Readers debate whether these were lawful sentences or a political purge; the chapter presents them as the way "the kingdom was firm in Solomon's hand" (1 Kings 2:46).

sections.h: Solomon, the anointed son of David (1 Kings 1–8)
sections.b: Solomon is the first son of David to be anointed (1 Kings 1:39) and the son of whom God said, "He will build a house for my name" (2 Samuel 7:13; 1 Kings 5:5; 8:19–20). His reign of peace, justice and wisdom, with the nations coming to hear him (1 Kings 4:34), became a pattern for the hope of a coming son of David: Psalm 72, titled "of Solomon," prays for such a king, and Isaiah 11 describes him with the Spirit of wisdom. The New Testament calls Jesus "son of David" and has Jesus say of himself, "here is something greater than Solomon" (Matthew 12:42).
sections.refs: 1 Kings 1:39; 1 Kings 4:34; 1 Kings 5:5; 1 Kings 8:19–20; 2 Samuel 7:12–14; Psalm 72; Isaiah 11:1–5; Matthew 12:42

sections.b: In the temple courtyard stood "the Sea," a great round basin of cast bronze, ten cubits (about 15 feet) across, holding two thousand baths (about 11,600 gallons), set on twelve bronze oxen facing the four directions (1 Kings 7:23–26). Chronicles says the priests washed in it (2 Chronicles 4:6). Its name suggests more: in the Bible the LORD rules the sea that other peoples feared as a god, and the temple's Sea may have stood for those waters, tamed and still. Revelation's sea "like glass" before God's throne is often compared (Revelation 4:6).
sections.refs: 1 Kings 7:23–26; 1 Kings 7:39; 1 Kings 7:44; 2 Chronicles 4:2–6; 2 Kings 16:17; 2 Kings 25:13; Revelation 4:6

sections.h: Turning back in Solomon's prayer (1 Kings 8)
sections.b: Solomon's prayer assumes that Israel will sin, "since there is no human being who never sins" (1 Kings 8:46), and makes repentance the way back: the people turn back to God, acknowledge his name, pray and plead toward his house (1 Kings 8:33, 8:35), "take it to heart" in a foreign land, and confess, "We have sinned. We have gone wrong. We have done evil" (1 Kings 8:47). The Hebrew plays on shuv, "turn back," again and again. God's part is to hear and forgive (1 Kings 8:30, 8:34, 8:36, 8:39, 8:50).

sections.h: The high places before the temple (1 Kings 3)
sections.b: Kings first mentions the high places with an excuse: the people sacrificed at them because, "up to that time, no house had been built for the LORD's name" (1 Kings 3:2). Solomon too "loved the LORD," only he sacrificed and burned offerings at the high places, and he went to Gibeon because "the greatest high place was there" (1 Kings 3:3–4). There God appeared to him in a dream (1 Kings 3:5). Deuteronomy allowed worship at many places only until the LORD gave rest and chose one place (Deuteronomy 12:8–14), and Solomon's temple is presented as that place (1 Kings 8:16, 8:29). From then on the high places are no longer excused, and Kings judges each king by whether he removed them (1 Kings 15:14; 2 Kings 23:8).
sections.refs: 1 Kings 3:2–5; 1 Kings 8:16; 1 Kings 8:29; 1 Kings 15:14; Deuteronomy 12:8–14; 2 Kings 23:8
